author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Boats That Return
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
Tomas came back on a rainy market morning, carrying a different suitcase.

I recognized him before he recognized me. The last time I'd seen him, he had been sitting on the steps of the north arch, frightened that accepting help meant he'd signed away his right to leave. He'd gone home with his destination kept private and no promise to return.

Now he stood under the bakery awning, studying a list of boat departures as though it were written in a language he hadn't practiced in years.

"Tomas?" I asked.

He turned.

His face changed slowly, from uncertainty to recognition.

"Jasper."

I smiled. "Welcome back."

He looked toward the square. The old arches glowed through the rain, and the scent of fresh bread moved past us every time Mara opened her door.

"Is that all?" he asked.

"What?"

"No questions about why I left? About whether I'm staying this time?"

"Would you like me to ask?"

He laughed once, startled. "No."

"Then I won't."

Maui appeared with a crate of sea kale for the pantry. He saw Tomas, stopped, and looked at me. I could see the memory pass across his face: Vel insisting that help created a debt, Tomas pulling his suitcase free, the quiet decision to let him go.

He straightened when he recognized Tomas. I watched the old welcome arrange itself on his face: broad shoulders, enormous grin, a greeting big enough to be heard across the cove.

"Ha! Look who's back! I told you this place was impossible to forget."

Tomas looked uncertain.

"Or," Maui added, catching himself, "you came because you wanted to. Also a perfectly respectable reason."

Mini Maui appeared over his heart and made a tiny, dramatic bow to the returning traveler. The gesture was ridiculous enough that Tomas almost smiled.

"You didn't come to inspect the famous demigod, did you?" Maui asked.

"No."

"Your loss. Excellent show. Limited seats."

I laughed. He set down the sea kale and let Tomas explain his plans without interrupting. He wanted the reassurance of knowing the traveler had missed us. Instead he listened to the real reason Tomas was here, and that mattered more.

When Tomas thanked him for letting him leave before, Maui flashed his usual grin.

"You're welcome. And if you do leave again, I reserve the right to miss your cooking. Not to stop you. Just to complain spectacularly about it."

"Hey," Maui said.

"Hey."

Maui set down the crate.

"Good to see you."

Tomas looked cautious. "You're not going to tell me I should have stayed?"

"No."

"Or that you were disappointed?"

"I'll admit it. The cove was more boring without you. I had to tell my best fishing story to a gull. Terrible audience." Maui shrugged, trying to look casual. "But a person isn't a fish you keep just because you hooked them. Wait. Terrible metaphor. Don't quote me."

Tomas stared at him.

Then he smiled.

They stood awkwardly for another second. Maui broke it by pointing at the suitcase.

"Need help with that?"

"Maybe later."

"All right."

He went to carry the kale inside.

It was such an ordinary exchange that I nearly cried.

Tomas had come back to visit, not to settle. He had a week's leave from work in his homeworld and wanted to see the coast again. He'd brought a small parcel of seeds for the sea-glass orchard, collected from a gardener who thought they might tolerate salt. He had not planted them yet; he wanted Fen's opinion first.

"Good," I said.

"I remembered you don't just put things in the ground because they look pretty."

"An excellent local tradition."

We walked to Tideglass after breakfast. The upper route was dry enough to use, though the lower maintenance passage remained closed and the old surface channel bore fresh inspection marks from the last storm.

Fen met us by the garden.

Tomas handed over the seed packet.

Fen read the label, asked about the plant's origin and growing conditions, then shook their head.

"Too aggressive for the dunes."

Tomas looked disappointed.

"But," Fen continued, "we could test a few in a contained pot, away from the native beds, with a plan to destroy them if they spread."

Tomas considered that.

"That sounds fair."

They wrote the trial conditions together.

Maui watched from the bench. He was carving another fish, this one with a rather thoughtful expression.

"You don't have to make him a present," I whispered.

"I wasn't going to."

I looked at the fish.

He sighed.

"Fine. I was going to ask first."

Progress came in strange shapes.

We ate lunch at the shelter overlooking the cove. Tomas told us about the work he'd found at home, repairing boats on a river that ran through his town. He spoke about his sister, who had been angry when he left without telling her exactly when he'd return. They'd had a difficult conversation and were still working through it.

"That sounds familiar," I said.

Maui looked at me.

I smiled.

Tomas asked whether the village had changed much.

I told him about the shared bridge maintenance plan, the archive's new access log, the three safe routes, the children-led Tidewake stage, and the Lantern Walk where people could carry blank lanterns without explaining what they meant. He listened with genuine curiosity.

Then he looked toward the north arch, far above the shoreline.

"I almost didn't come back," he said.

"Why?" Maui asked.

"Because I thought people would make it a lesson. Look, the boy who left realized he belonged here after all."

I felt my stomach tighten.

"And?" I asked.

"And I realized I could visit without proving anyone right. I wanted to see the water. I wanted to bring seeds. That's enough."

"Yes," I said.

Maui nodded.

"It is."

Before we reached the market, Tomas asked whether the little boat he had helped repair last year was still in service.

"Lio's skiff?" Maui said. "Yes. It's carrying tools now."

Tomas looked delighted. "I remember the cracked seat. I thought it would be easier to replace the whole thing."

"Lio disagreed," I said. "She has a talent for disagreeing when people suggest spending money she doesn't have."

We walked down to the mooring. Lio recognized Tomas and showed him the replacement seat, with its reinforcement underneath. He asked whether he could help unload the day's crate. She said the crew had already been paid for the job, but if he wanted to visit her workshop later she could show him the way they'd repaired the frame.

"I'd like that," he said. "If it's not inconvenient."

"Ask on Thursday. I'm closed tomorrow."

He smiled at the plain answer. A year before, he would have heard it as a refusal to welcome him.

Maui hung back beside the rope bins.

"He's coming back for a workshop," he murmured.

"Maybe. He said he'd ask."

"Would it be wrong to hope he does?"

"No. It would be wrong to turn the hope into a debt."

Maui looked at the fish he'd been carving. "I suppose I'll finish this whether he takes it or not."

"Then perhaps you're making it because you like making fish."

He considered the possibility with exaggerated suspicion. "A terrible discovery."

We laughed. His shoulder pressed lightly against mine, and for a few seconds I imagined the rest of the evening without a council meeting or weather warning. I would spend another day with people I loved elsewhere; Maui knew that, and he had his own friends and tasks. We didn't need a single household to consume every other obligation.

When we turned back toward the market, I could hear vendors calling out today's prices. The sounds were the same as always. Tomas had returned to find a place that had continued existing after he left, and a place that would keep existing after he went home again.

I thought that was a kinder welcome than any parade.

A little later we saw Vel at the market. She had repaired her cart after the storm and was selling small woven baskets. Tomas stopped when he recognized her.

I expected something dramatic.

Vel looked at him, then at the basket in her hands.

"Hello," she said.

"Hello."

A long pause.

"I'm glad you reached home safely," she added.

"Thank you."

Neither demanded an apology from the other. Neither pretended their disagreement had disappeared. Tomas bought a basket, paid the marked price, and went on his way.

I looked at Maui.

He was watching with an expression I couldn't read.

"Do you want to talk?" I asked.

"Not yet."

I nodded.

We spent the afternoon checking the tide markers. Tomas asked Fen whether he could help carry the small inspection kit. Fen agreed, gave him clear instructions, and thanked him when the work was done.

Nobody gave him a badge for returning.

Nobody wrote his name on the public board unless he chose to claim a shift.

At dusk, he told us he was leaving again in six days.

Maui looked up from the carving.

"Okay."

Tomas blinked.

"Okay?"

"Would you like help planning the route?"

"Yes."

"Then we'll ask Neri for the current map. You can choose the escort."

Tomas smiled.

That evening, I found Maui by the old signal post. He held the finished wooden fish in his palm.

"Going to give it to him?" I asked.

"Only if he wants it."

"Good."

He looked at me.

"I thought I'd feel proud that he came back."

"Do you?"

"A little. But mostly I'm glad he felt free enough to."

I took his hand.

"The invitation matters more when it can be refused."

He nodded.

Below us, Lio's skiff returned to the landing with a small cargo of tools. The boat moved steadily through the water, its lantern swinging gently from the bow. Fen checked the mooring, and the people on shore stepped aside to let the crew unload.

Lio had a folded coastal chart tucked beneath the ropes. He called up to Maui before unloading, asking whether the familiar handwriting belonged to someone he knew.

Maui took the page and broke into a grin. "Oh, that's her. Only one person I know corrects my work with this much enthusiasm."

The chart came from Moana. It marked a reef approach in her own waters and asked for a comparison with a current measurement Maui had once boasted about. The note was brief and entirely about the voyage: a crew needed safe bearings before the next weather change, and the answer had to reach them while it was still useful.

"Does she want you to go?" I asked.

"No. She wants a reading, not a dramatic entrance."

He sounded offended by the distinction. I was beginning to understand that his affection for Moana had always included the irritation of respecting somebody who could out-argue him at sea.

We took the chart to Fen instead of guessing from memory. Fen checked the date and offered a measurement range with the uncertainty written beside it. Maui supplied the part he knew from the route he'd actually traveled. Neither pretended that Lanternweald's tides were the same as Moana's homewaters.

Maui drew an enormous flourish beside his figures, paused and crossed it out.

"Too much?" he asked.

"For a navigation chart?"

He sighed. "Some audiences are impossible."

He kept the signature small. Lio agreed to carry the reply only after confirming his own return route and schedule. Moana would make the navigational decision with her crew. Maui was free to be proud of helping without owning what happened next.

Boats came back because their captains chose to steer home.

That night, Maui placed the fish on the shelf.

He would ask Tomas tomorrow.

Either answer would be all right.
